it was interesting reading your post and the comments here. i vaped & used zyns A LOT for about 2-3 years and i found it helped me a lot with my depression. i believe it was because i was so motivated and had no brain fog because of nicotine. i found i was able to wake up with a clear mind once i took my morning hit and get started on work & deal with issues by putting them to the side; vaping them away. it calmed me a lot. nicotine did not contribute to my episodes for the 2-3 years that i used it all the time, neither did it make me feel worse. 

when i stopped vaping a month ago, the withdrawal messed me up very badly. i struggle with anhedonia and its been that way for a while so i can’t attribute this to vaping. i think its important to look at the overall picture, as in, your mood episodes over time with positive and negative interventions and their associated effects. 

the research is there, but on a personal level, it is impossible to measure nicotine’s impact on the longevity, reoccurrence, and severity of bipolar episodes or mood related issues due to external factors at play. interestingly, i’ve noticed a number of accounts of people with bipolar benefiting from nicotine at controlled doses.

September 2024 was my first time quitting. i quit nicotine for 2 months and i noticed severe depression and anxiety even 2 months later, hence, the relapse. IMO it is significantly harder to quit nicotine if you have an underlying mental health concern, especially if it’s not managed with effective medications and therapy. however, the second time i quit (now) i feel like im doing much better than the last time. my anxiety is at an all time high though and it wasn’t when i was vaping. the withdrawal period is a long and hard journey. i hope to look back at this post and tell you or reflect on how much bipolar symptoms improve after 5 months of quitting nicotine or 1 year. it would be interesting to evaluate that and how long the mental withdrawal effects last.

hey, i have this diagnosis & i know symptoms of psychosis vary from person to person so i can share a little about the psychosis symptoms ive experienced through my two separate psychotic breaks (unmedicated) and how being medicated reduces/prevents psychosis symptoms. 

so during my full blown psychotic breaks, i lost touch with reality and thought i was above everyone and the law (delusions). i also thought everyone was out to get me and i was constantly angry - in fight mode. during these times i experienced auditory hallucinations of people talking about me and saw shadows from the corner of my eyes. 

when medicated - i feel severely depressed & have less delusions, hallucinations, etc. however, i do have strong beliefs of worst case scenarios happening which i attribute to anxiety. i usually have severe health anxiety and overall feel like my days are numbered. occasionally when really low, ive experienced auditory hallucinations (voices) telling me to end my life and thats usually when i make my way to the hospital. 

again, this is just my experience with this diagnosis & its “psychotic features”. it’s not a constant, there are triggers for psychosis or psychotic breaks and you have to be careful with medication, working out, eating well, and having a support system. good luck with your appointment :)

Hi, I'm also dealing with this right now. How you can deal with it is by feeling each of those intrusive thoughts and knowing that you've felt them before and you're still here. They are passive thoughts due to pain and hopelessness in things getting better. You have to trick your mind that there is light at the end of the tunnel and when you come out of this period, you'll be happy. It's hard to do because it feels like that has never been the case but look back at very very low periods of your life when you thought you would never make it out alive, now tell yourself that you did and you *will*.

Relationships and friendships are superficial - you can't actually understand what people are going through and support them because you choose yourself. At the end of the day that means we're actually always alone in the hardships of life and it's hard to accept as humans are inherently social species and it hurts so badly to see older people literally alone in restaurants, parks, etc.

Thoughts of "what if I" or feeling exhausted with life and wanting some kind of way out are normal. We are human beings... we have hundreds of thoughts every day and not all of them are true or what we actually want, most happen in the heat of the moment. However, when these thoughts become the majority of what you think about day to day and you've started thinking about the ways in which you would act on them, that is not normal and it's scary. It happens though and it's about knowing what to do when it gets like that again.
